title: A new technique for generating quadratic programming test problems
contribution: A unified, subproblem-free generator of convex, strictly concave, bilinear and indefinite QP test problems with known minima, built from separable two-variable blocks and disguised by a sparse Householder-diagonal change of variables.
problem_entry: Existing QP generators need LPs, convex programs or linear systems and put the global minimum at a vertex, which favours vertex-visiting algorithms; none produce jointly constrained bilinear problems (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Direct sum of m two-variable blocks whose minima are read off their geometry; block data select the class; separability hidden by M = DH (random sparse Householder H, diagonal D with chosen conditioning) (pp. 3-9).
assumptions: Linear constraints, quadratic objective; distinct local-minimum values need certain powers of 4 built from l and L to stay machine-distinguishable from 0 and 1, which bounds L (pp. 4, 12); active gradients linearly independent at all minima (pp. 5, 7, 9).
proof_devices: per-block minima from 2-D geometry, combined by separability (pp. 3-9)
induction on value gaps: next block's smallest gap exceeds the sum of earlier blocks' largest gaps via geometric scaling (Property 3.2, p. 5)
one-to-one correspondence of strong local minima under a nonsingular linear transformation (Propositions 4.1-4.3, pp. 9-10)
nonzero counts and condition number of the transformed data from v and D (Propositions 4.4-4.5, pp. 10-11)
experiments: none; worked example with m = 3, n = 6, 18 local minima incl. 2 global, before and after transformation (pp. 12-13).
positioning: Reviews Rosen-Suzuki, Rosen, Sung-Rosen, Kalantari-Rosen, Pardalos, Hager et al. and Kalantari by their computational cost and minimum location, and claims to be the only bilinear generator (pp. 1-2).
writing: Numbered 'Property' statements after each construction; the contribution is stated as the list of hard features the generator can produce (p. 2); the conclusion opens with a benchmarking-care sentence (p. 14).
limits_future: Concrete: removing constraints makes the region non-closed; the floating-point bound on L caps the number of minima (two remedies sketched); the full transform destroys bilinearity unless M is block diagonal (pp. 11-12); no algorithm is run on the problems.

method_links.note: Early release of benchmark infrastructure (generator + Fortran code on request), not a solver; no profiles.
Conclusion stresses care in testing, benchmarking and interpreting results.
Construction-level analogue: the block-plus-transformation skeleton is reused from the bilevel generator; only block data change per class.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Generator with a selectable number and type of minima, nonextreme global minima and exponentially many local minima; code released.
Every minimum of every generated instance is known by construction.

transferable: Build known-minimum test problems as a direct sum of 2-D blocks, then disguise with z = W z_bar, W = M^-1 = H D^-1, M = DH (sparse random Householder H, diagonal D with chosen condition number); sparsity of v sets density, D sets conditioning (pp. 3, 9-11).
Scale block l geometrically so each block's smallest value gap exceeds the sum of all earlier blocks' largest gaps; all local minima then have distinct values (p. 5).
Place global minima at nonextreme points so vertex-enumerating methods cannot exploit the generator (pp. 2, 7, 9).
coauthors: P. H. Calamai, J. J. Júdice

quotes.text: Unlike most existing methods our construction technique does not require the solution of any subproblems or systems of equations.
Care must be exercised in the testing and benchmarking of algorithms and in the interpretation and dissemination of the corresponding results [4, 5, 14].

title: Algorithm 728: FORTRAN subroutines for generating quadratic bilevel programming test problems
contribution: Portable FORTRAN 77 suite implementing the Calamai-Vicente quadratic bilevel test-problem generator, with an evaluator, a solution checker against all known minimizers, an installation test and usage examples.
problem_entry: No other technique generates quadratic bilevel test problems; the codes are offered for testing, verifying and comparing methods (p. 1).
key_idea: Central generator qbpgen with user knobs (level sizes, solution characteristics m1-m4, transformation condition and nonzeros) plus qbpchk, which checks a candidate against all minimizers in the untransformed space (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Not applicable (software); ANSI FORTRAN 77, level-1 BLAS, Schrage random number generator; maxn = 2000 (pp. 2, 4).
experiments: none; installation test program 'verify' and example program 'usage' (pp. 3-4).
positioning: Companion to Calamai and Vicente (1994) in the same TOMS issue; claims no competing generator (p. 1).
writing: Short ACM algorithm note: routine list, usage notes, installation notes, limitations (pp. 1-4).
limits_future: Concrete: maximum problem size fixed at maxn = 2000 in parameter statements (p. 4); no future work.

method_links.note: Earliest instance of the release habit: a citable software paper with installation test; ships a generator, not a solver.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: infrastructure as a stand-alone citable publication (existing c2-02 candidate)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Separate ACM TOMS algorithm paper for the generator code.
User-controlled number and type of minima and conditioning/sparsity of the disguise.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: theory paper / application paper split (existing c05 candidate), variant
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Split into method paper (S026) and software paper (D001) in the same issue.

transferable: Ship a solution checker with a generator: map the candidate back to the untransformed space and return the nearest known minimizer, the distance and its type (p. 3).
Expose the difficulty knobs (number and type of minima, conditioning and sparsity of the disguising transformation) as generator arguments (p. 2).
Include a verification program and a usage program with annotated example calls (pp. 3-4).

quotes.text: Our hope is that these codes will be used for testing, verifying, and comparing new (and established) solution methods.
To encourage the use of these codes, every effort has been made to keep them as flexible as possible.

title: Generating quadratic bilevel programming test problems
contribution: A subproblem-free generator of sparse or dense quadratic bilevel test problems with a selectable number of known global and local solutions, whose global solutions differ from the relaxed-QP solution in a selectable number of variables and which satisfy the assumptions of three solution-method families.
problem_entry: No standardized quadratic bilevel test problems exist although many methods are proposed; most methods start from the relaxed QP (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Separable parametric QBP of two-variable one-parameter blocks with four cases in rho_k; combine block solutions; disguise with a block-diagonal Householder-diagonal transformation that keeps the upper/lower split (pp. 3-13).
assumptions: Upper level convex quadratic, lower level strictly convex in y, linear constraints, no upper-level constraints (pp. 15-16).
proof_devices: KKT case analysis showing the induced region is a union of three segments, with contradictions from multiplier signs (Proposition 1, pp. 5-6)
level-circle argument around the relaxed minimizer (1,0) to identify global and local block minimizers (pp. 8-9)
combinatorial counting over blocks: 2^{m3} global and 2^{m2+m3+m4} - 2^{m3} additional local solutions (Properties 1-2, pp. 9-10)
experiments: none; §8 example (nx = 4, ny = 2) with global value 0.3125 and 3 extra local solutions (pp. 13-15); §9 checks the assumptions of branch-and-bound, steepest-descent and exact-penalty methods (pp. 15-16).
positioning: Cites NLP generators (Floudas-Pardalos, Kalantari-Rosen, Lenard-Minkoff) as not addressing bilevel problems; positions against the requirements of Edmunds-Bard, Gauvin-Savard and Bi-Calamai-Conn (pp. 2, 15-16).
writing: Abstract lists the controllable features; numbered PROPERTY statements with one-paragraph reasons; conclusion opens with a criterion for useful test problems (pp. 1, 9-10, 15).
limits_future: Few limits stated (a bounded region needs x_k >= 0, p. 16); future: generators for linear and linear-quadratic bilevel problems (p. 16).

method_links.note: Early benchmark infrastructure with code released separately (D001); no solver, no profiles.
The same block-plus-transformation skeleton moves from bilevel (S026) to single-level QP (S053).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Selectable numbers of global and local solutions and control of sparsity and conditioning.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: aim the benchmark at the solvers' first move and certify it against their assumptions
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Global solution made to differ from the relaxed-QP solution most methods compute first; §9 proves the instances meet three method families' assumptions.

transferable: Make the global solution differ from the obvious warm start (the relaxation's solution) in a controlled number of variables (p. 1; Property 3, p. 10).
Before releasing a benchmark, list each target solver family's standing assumptions and verify them item by item for the generated instances (pp. 15-16).
Keep structure through a random disguise by making the transformation block-diagonal along the structure (separate Householder factors for upper- and lower-level variables) (p. 12).

quotes.text: the global solutions are constructed to be different than the global solution of this relaxed problem in a selectable number of upper- and lower-level variables.
Test problems are only useful when they can be used to test solution techniques.

title: Local convergence of the affine-scaling interior-point algorithm for nonlinear programming
contribution: Local q-linear, q-superlinear (Dennis-More) and q-quadratic convergence of the Coleman-Li affine-scaling interior-point algorithm for nonlinear programming, with quasi-Newton Hessians and inexact linear solves.
problem_entry: Local theory exists for primal-dual IPMs but not, in general, for affine-scaling IPMs; the paper fills this gap and excludes global convergence and polynomiality (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Eliminate bound multipliers with the Coleman-Li scaling D(x, lambda); freeze the scaling's branch by the limit point so the step is a quasi-Newton step for a Lipschitz-differentiable system; then reuse the classical quasi-Newton theory (pp. 3, 6-7).
assumptions: f, g twice Lipschitz continuously differentiable; regular x*, strict complementarity, second-order sufficiency; bounded deterioration of H_k for q-linear; parameter and residual decay in powers of ||F(w_k)|| per rate (pp. 4, 10-11).
proof_devices: Lemma 3.1: bound |1 - alpha_k| <= |1 - tau_k| + tau_k(c2||dw_k|| + c3||s1_k||) by splitting inactive (distance to boundary) and active (strict complementarity, (E_k)_ii >= (E*)_ii/2) indices (pp. 7-8)
Lemma 3.2: A_k nonsingular and close to grad F(w*) via add-and-subtract in the Frobenius norm (p. 9)
error decomposition (21) of w_{k+1} - w* feeding the Broyden-Dennis-More / Yamashita-Yabe argument; proofs omitted as similar (pp. 8, 10)
positioning: Follows Yamashita-Yabe's primal-dual analysis and Broyden-Dennis-More / Dennis-More quasi-Newton theory; surveys primal-dual and affine-scaling IPM literature, noting Heinkenschloss-Ulbrich-Ulbrich avoid strict complementarity for bounds (pp. 1-2, 10).
writing: Gap statement in the author's voice (no general affine-scaling analysis), explicit scope exclusion, three rate theorems in parallel form; no conclusion section (pp. 2, 10-11).
limits_future: Local only: no global convergence or polynomiality (p. 2); strict complementarity assumed; no future work (paper ends at Theorem 4.3, p. 11).

method_links.note: Quasi-Newton local-theory skeleton kept; only the Newton system changes to the affine-scaled one; technical lemmas obtained differently from Yamashita-Yabe.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: bridge inequality to a classical proof (existing s01 candidate)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Two lemmas plug into the Yamashita-Yabe / Dennis-More argument whose proofs are then omitted as similar; now also in S037, S031, S039, S085.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: deterministic inexactness tied to the step (existing s2-03 candidate), variant
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Residual of the inexact linear solve must decay as a power of ||F(w_k)||, one tolerance per target rate.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: branch-freezing to smooth a piecewise map near the solution
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Modified scaling D[x*, lambda*, k] coincides with D near the solution and is Lipschitz differentiable, so smooth quasi-Newton theory applies.

transferable: If a reformulated KKT map is nondifferentiable where a component of the Lagrangian gradient vanishes, define a surrogate whose branch is fixed by the limit point and current iterate; near the solution it equals the algorithm's map and is Lipschitz differentiable (pp. 6-7).
State one rate theorem per level (linear, superlinear, quadratic), each with the required decay of every algorithm parameter written in ||F(w_k)|| (pp. 10-11).
Bound a fraction-to-boundary step deficit by treating inactive and active indices separately, using strict complementarity for the active ones (pp. 7-8).

quotes.text: The proofs are similar and are omitted.

title: Matemática industrial em Portugal. Análise e perspectivas
contribution: A policy essay (in Portuguese) diagnosing industrial mathematics in Portugal in research and teaching, graduate careers and academia-industry collaboration, with concrete academic and national proposals.
problem_entry: Mathematics is used in all sciences and technologies (SIAM 1998 report); the essay asks how industrial mathematics stands in Portugal under three stated aspects (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: The pure/applied split is artificial; applications come from the researcher's own internationally demanding research portfolio and personal contacts; training in industrial mathematics needs mathematics, scientific computing and other disciplines' language; problems arrive unformulated (pp. 2, 4-6).
assumptions: Evidence base: SIAM report (200+ industrial staff), 2002 Coimbra study of firms in the Centro region, 2005 Coimbra Industrial Workshop, 2002-2004 evaluation panel (pp. 1-2, 4).
positioning: Measures Portugal against the SIAM report and other countries' institutes (ZIB, IMA, ECMI study groups); credits the Portuguese OR community as more dynamic than mathematics (pp. 2-3).
writing: Numbered contents, diagnosis before prescription, each institutional option weighed by impact vs feasibility, frank judgments of academic culture (pp. 1, 4, 6-7).
limits_future: Concedes the proposals are not original; weighs a cheaper option as lacking the needed energy; agenda of national initiatives (pp. 6-7).

method_links.note: Stated: industrial applications come from the academic's own research portfolio and personal contacts, not goodwill.
Stated: mastery of scientific-computing tools is an essential part of industrial-mathematics training; a second stated source beside the 2018 Lehigh quote.
Stated background: industrial problems arrive unformulated, with blurred borders and diffuse goals, so formulation is part of the work.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: applications through one's own research network
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Stated belief that applications grow from the researcher's own demanding research portfolio and personal contacts over years; practice evidence must come from the application papers.

transferable: Open a perspective or policy piece by stating the aspects to be analysed and back each with a cited survey or report (p. 2).
Weigh each proposed option by impact against feasibility and name the cheaper option's weakness (pp. 6-7).

quotes.text: Elas estão agregadas a uma carteira profissional de investigação dos professores e investigadores académicos, exigente no plano internacional e aberta na ligação às demais ciências.
Os problemas na Matemática Industrial não aparecem formulados, prontos a serem submetidos a uma intervenção retirada à pressa de um livro de receitas.

title: Using simplex gradients of nonsmooth functions in direct search methods
contribution: Shows that limits of simplex gradients along refining subsequences of GPS/MADS give estimates of Clarke generalized directional derivatives (and converge to the gradient under strict differentiability), and confirms numerically that simplex-gradient poll ordering saves evaluations on nonsmooth problems.
problem_entry: Simplex-gradient poll ordering was shown to help for smooth problems and simplex-gradient accuracy is known only for smooth f, while GPS/MADS have nonsmooth convergence theory (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Analyse simplex gradients built from Lambda-poised subsets of the poll points at unsuccessful iterates with alpha_k -> 0, compare their limits with Clarke derivatives, and use them for poll ordering and a stopping test (pp. 3-10).
assumptions: f Lipschitz near x*; iterates in a compact set; |D_k| bounded; alpha_k||d_k|| -> 0; strict differentiability at x* for the gradient-convergence result (pp. 3-5, 8).
proof_devices: boundedness of simplex gradients from Lipschitz continuity and Lambda-poisedness (Lemma 3.1, p. 4)
limit comparison with Clarke's generalized directional derivative f°(x*; v) >= grad_s f*^T v, plus a least-squares residual term in the overdetermined case (Theorems 3.2-3.3, pp. 5-7)
Lipschitz mean value theorem with Clarke subgradients, closedness and local boundedness of the subdifferential (Theorem 3.5, pp. 8-9)
poisedness bounded by the cosine measure ||Sigma^-1|| <= 1/(d_min kappa(D)) via Courant-Fischer (Proposition 1, p. 10)
LTMADS poisedness Lambda = n 2^{n-1} from a triangular-inverse norm bound (pp. 11-12)
experiments: 14 nonsmooth problems (n = 5-50); coordinate search with and without simplex-gradient ordering; per-problem evaluations and final values; about 27% fewer evaluations on average, small increases on some problems (pp. 12-13).
positioning: Extends Custódio-Vicente [8] from smooth to nonsmooth; builds on Audet-Dennis GPS/MADS refining-subsequence analysis and Conn-Scheinberg-Vicente Lambda-poisedness (pp. 1-4).
writing: Twofold purpose stated in the abstract; theorems followed by candid remarks on their scope ('a first step'); explicit comparison with the smooth-case gain (pp. 1, 7, 13).
limits_future: Overdetermined result only a first step; underdetermined case of little interest; no gradient convergence with fewer than n+1 points; simplex-gradient stopping behaves like the mesh-size test; no future work (pp. 5, 7, 9, 13).

method_links.note: The ordering heuristic lives in the poll-ordering slot not used by the convergence theory; the paper supplies theory for why it stays informative for nonsmooth f.
Theory that explains the numerics: Clarke-derivative estimates justify the observed savings.
All previously evaluated points are candidates for the simplex gradient (store-all).
Stated collection and ablation against the same method without ordering; no profiles, no external baseline, no code mention.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: state where you lose (existing c05 candidate)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The new stopping test is reported as no better than the mesh-size test; the gain (27%) is compared with the larger smooth-case gain (50%); increases are shown.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: import model-geometry theory into direct search (existing c03 candidate)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lambda-poisedness tied to the cosine measure of positive spanning sets.

transferable: Validate a sample-based gradient surrogate at nonsmooth points by taking its limit along refining subsequences and comparing with Clarke's generalized directional derivative (pp. 5-7).
Bound the poisedness of a poll set by its cosine measure, ||Sigma^-1|| <= 1/(d_min kappa(D)), to reuse interpolation error bounds in any method with a cosine-measure guarantee (p. 10).
Use the Lipschitz mean value theorem with Clarke subgradients plus closedness and local boundedness of the subdifferential to pass finite-difference quantities to the limit (pp. 5, 8-9).
Report an add-on ablation with per-problem evaluations and final values so cheaper-but-worse runs are visible (p. 13).
coauthors: A. L. Custódio, J. E. Dennis Jr.

quotes.text: Theorem 3.3 should be primarily regarded as a first step to understand the use of overdetermined simplex gradients in the nonsmooth setting.

Our numerical experience has shown, however, that the use of this stopping criterion has an effect similar to the use of a stopping criterion in which the algorithm would stop if the size of αk follows below a prescribed tolerance.

title: SID-PSM: A pattern search method guided by simplex derivatives for use in derivative-free optimization
contribution: User manual of the SID-PSM v1.3 MATLAB solver (LGPL): generalized pattern search with simplex-derivative poll ordering, MFN-model search step, simplex-gradient stopping and mesh options, with installation, running and parameter documentation.
problem_entry: Derivative-free minimization of black-box f over R^n or {c_i(x) <= 0} with constraint gradients supplied; distinguishing feature vs NOMAD/NOMADm and APPSPACK is reuse of past evaluations (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: GPS with italicized additions: Lambda-poised sets from stored points give simplex derivatives and a descent indicator for ordering/pruning/stopping/mesh update; MFN quadratic models drive the search step (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: Theory for global convergence to stationary points except in the nonlinear constrained case; mesh projection of the model minimizer not implemented; pruning conditions untested (pp. 2, 6, 8).
experiments: no benchmark; demonstration on (x2 - x1^2)^2 from (-1.2, 1): 145 evaluations unconstrained, 129 with bounds (pp. 11, 17-19).
positioning: Contrasted with NOMAD/NOMADm (dynamic polling; NOMADm 4.6 adopts a simplified SID-PSM strategy) and APPSPACK (pp. 2-4).
writing: Algorithm box with the additions to GPS in italic; per-option parameter table with defaults and ranges; citation request in the abstract (pp. 1, 4-5, 20-22).
limits_future: Concrete: MATLAB only, constraint gradients required, no theory for nonlinear constraints, missing mesh projection, prudent use of pruning, degenerate constraint gradients halt the run (pp. 2, 6, 8-9, 13); no future work.

method_links.note: The released artefact: LGPL, install notes, drivers, parameters file, per-file documentation, citation request; every strategy is a switchable option, matching Step 1.
Search step free of rules hosts the MFN model and the poll carries convergence, but the glue is the mesh with simple decrease; sufficient decrease is only a mesh-update option (c03 correction).
Past evaluations feed simplex derivatives and MFN models at no extra evaluation cost.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: No theory for nonlinear constraints; mesh projection not implemented; pruning conditions never tested.

transferable: Typeset in the algorithm box exactly what differs from the base method whose theory you inherit (Fig. 2.1, pp. 4-5).
Expose each heuristic as a numbered option with default and range in one parameters file, so users and later papers can run ablations (pp. 20-22).
Put a citation request naming the method papers in the software manual's abstract (p. 1).
Cache evaluated points and match candidates with an l1 prefilter then an l-infinity tolerance before evaluating (pp. 8, 14).
Ship unconstrained and constrained toy drivers and print their expected output in appendices (pp. 11, 17-19).

quotes.text: The search step is free of any rules as long as only a finite number of (feasible) trial points in the current mesh is considered.
Note that for global convergence purposes the minimizer should be projected onto the mesh. However, this projection is not implemented in SID-PSM.
